findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) will become the overriding Transformation Programme on its own and will take significant resource to deliver... a specific reserve has been created to mitigate such risks (£2.9m by March 2028)

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for Budget and Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Council Tax freeze for 2026/27 sacrifices £0.222m immediate income and £1.225m over the five-year period, perpetuating Rushcliffe's below-average tax position.
findings.detail: The council has chosen to freeze the Rushcliffe element of council tax for 2026/27 (saving residents £4.59/annum), despite government funding assumptions assuming councils will maximize increases at 2.99%. This forgoes £0.222m in 2026/27 and £1.225m over five years. The council notes it is 'already in the lowest 25% of district councils for its element of Council Tax' and that freezing 'perpetuates an existing inequality within the current funding system' while reducing future Council Tax income, 'one of its more stable income streams.'
findings.matters: A lender assesses revenue stability; council tax is one of the most predictable streams. By freezing, the council reduces its future raising capacity and locks in a lower baseline for many years. This is a policy choice to forgo revenue, not a financial necessity.
findings.figures: £0.222m immediate loss (2026/27); £1.225m loss over five years; £4.59 per annum saving for residents
findings.quote: if the Council were to increase by the full 3% this would be a total increase of £5.47, with Rushcliffe's element £4.59 or 2.84%, by choosing to freeze Council Tax for 2026/27, income of £0.222m is foregone and this represents a loss of £1.225m over the 5 years

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for Budget and Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Five-year medium-term financial plan shows £0.815m cumulative deficit, minimal in-year surplus by 2030/31, and reserves heavily committed to Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.detail: The council projects a net deficit of £0.815m over the five-year MTFS period. The deficit 'includes two years of transition grant and by 2030 the in-year surplus is minimal.' While reserves are reasonable at £24.9m by 2030/31, 'most reserves have specifically identified uses such as for LGR which are not yet reflected in the budget and so financial risk remains significant.' A specific reserve of £2.9m has been created by March 2028 for LGR-related costs (recruitment, retention, agency resource, systems changes).
findings.matters: The council is not running a true operating surplus; it is drawing down earmarked reserves to balance the budget. The accumulation of reserves for future LGR costs means those reserves cannot be deployed for unexpected pressures. By 2030/31, the in-year position is precarious.
findings.figures: £0.815m five-year deficit; £24.9m reserves by 2030/31; £2.9m LGR reserve by March 2028
findings.quote: the net projected financial position over the 5 years gives a £0.815m deficit. The deficit includes two years of transition grant and by 2030 the in-year surplus is minimal... most reserves have specifically identified uses such as for LGR which are not yet reflected in the budget and so financial risk remains significant

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for Budget and Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Simpler Recycling new burden has uncertain future funding; estimated costs of £1.5m by 2030/31 against only £1.279m indicated for 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council is implementing Simpler Recycling (kerbside glass 2025/26, kerbside food 2027/28) funded by Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) grants. However, there are 'uncertainties around the level of funding' as producers minimize their EPR levy through packaging changes, which reduces EPR grants to local authorities. Costs are estimated at £1.5m by 2030/31, creating a growing funding gap. A Simpler Recycling Reserve was created and replenished by £1.25m in 2028/29 but 'may need to be topped-up for future years if additional funding is not secured.'
findings.matters: This is a government-mandated service with no guaranteed funding mechanism. The council must fund a growing shortfall from reserves or revenue. It exemplifies the unfunded new burdens councils face and represents a call on reserves that limits other financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £1.279m indicated 2026/27; costs estimated £1.5m by 2030/31; reserve replenished £1.25m in 2028/29
findings.quote: There remain uncertainties around the level of funding with an indication of £1.279m for 2026/27 and the expectation that this will reduce as producers seek to minimise the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) charge... With costs of these increased collections estimated at £1.5m by 2030/31, it is clear that there will be both significant revenue and capital pressures... may need to be topped-up for future years if additional funding is not secured

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for Budget and Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Loss of £1.478m New Homes Bonus funding with no replacement, rolled into Revenue Support Grant as part of Fair Funding.
findings.detail: New Homes Bonus, a 'significant funding stream for the Borough (regularly circa £1.5m or more)', has been consolidated into the Revenue Support Grant as part of the Fair Funding Review. The 2025/26 payment of £1.478m is effectively removed from 2026/27 onwards, though theoretically rolled into redistributed RSG (which also decreased).
findings.matters: A large, previously predictable income stream is eliminated. The council loses both the cash and the link between housing growth incentives and council finances, reducing flexibility to invest in growth infrastructure.
findings.quote: loss of New Homes Bonus, which was a significant funding stream for the Borough (regularly circa £1.5m or more)

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for Budget and Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Business Rates income collapses 60% in 2026/27 due to rates reset, from £6.676m to £2.675m, though transitional grants provide short-term cover.
findings.detail: The government's business rates reset and Fair Funding Review reset business rates baselines. Rushcliffe's retained business rates drop from £6.676m in 2025/26 to £2.675m in 2026/27. However, a one-year adjustment grant (£0.484m) and transition grants totalling £1.115m across 2027/28-2028/29 offset the impact in the short term, providing only 95% funding floor protection. No protection beyond 2028/29.
findings.matters: A structural cut of this magnitude to a major revenue stream represents significant financial risk, even with transitional protection. By 2030/31, the council must operate with 60% less retained business rates than in 2025/26.
findings.quote: The effect of the reset is a reduction from £6.676m in Business Rates income in 2025/26 to £2.675m in 2026/27 a 60% reduction

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for Budget and Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Rushcliffe is 'one of the worst authorities affected' by Fair Funding Review with core spending power reduction of 2.25% to 2028/29, rising to 4.12% if council tax is frozen.
findings.detail: The government's Fair Funding Review redistributes funding based on relative need and deprivation, disadvantaging more financially stable districts like Rushcliffe. The council faces a reduction in Core Spending Power of 2.25% between 2025/26 and 2028/29, and receives only 95% funding floor protection rather than the 100% protection many other district councils will receive. Freezing council tax (which the council has chosen to do) increases this reduction to 4.12%.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that Rushcliffe's income position is deteriorating in real terms despite being prudently managed, and that government funding cannot be relied upon to grow. The council's room for maneuver is shrinking.
findings.figures: 2.25% CSP reduction 2025/26 to 2028/29; 4.12% reduction with tax freeze; 95% funding floor vs 100% for other councils
findings.quote: Rushcliffe is one of the worst authorities affected seeing a reduction in core spending power of 2.25% between 2025/26 and 2028/29

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will likely occur before end of current five-year plan
findings.detail: The MTFS is written for five years (to 2030/31) but the council expects to be operating under a new unitary council structure before the strategy period ends. This creates material uncertainty over the viability and scope of the plan, with the Transformation Plan expected to undergo iterative revision.
findings.matters: Structural reorganisation introduces binary risk: plans may be disrupted, roles may change, and financial baselines could shift unexpectedly, affecting a lender's ability to model the council's future state.
findings.figures: MTFS period: 2026/27 to 2030/31; LGR expected before end of period
findings.quote: Whilst this MTFS has been prepared for a five-year period, it is likely that the Council will be operating under a new unitary council before the end of this MTFS period.

findings.headline: Efficiency plan delivers £1.998m savings but leaves £0.815m net deficit over the five-year period
findings.detail: Despite identifying £1.998m in efficiencies, the Transformation and Efficiency Plan results in a net five-year deficit of £0.815m. The Organisation Stabilisation Reserve is being used to smooth fluctuations, but with LGR uncertainty ahead, the plan will require iterative revision.
findings.matters: The shortfall shows the council cannot close its structural gap with identified savings alone and must rely on reserves, raising questions about sustainability.
findings.figures: £1.998m efficiencies; £0.815m net deficit
findings.quote: the Transformation and Efficiency Plan (TEP) delivers £1.998m of efficiencies over the five-year period, with a net deficit of £0.815m. The Organisation Stabilisation Reserve will be used to smooth the effect of variation in net budget requirement.

findings.headline: Business Rates income collapses by 60% due to national reset
findings.detail: Business Rates retained income fell from £6.676m in 2025/26 to £2.675m in 2026/27 as part of the Fair Funding Review's national reset. A transition grant partially offsets this in later years, but the reduction is permanent. The Nottinghamshire Business Rates Pool is being dissolved due to increased risk.
findings.matters: A £4m revenue loss in a single year is material and signals structural income weakness that lenders would scrutinise closely.
findings.quote: Business Rates have undergone a national reset as part of the Fair Funding Review, resulting in a significant reduction in retained income—from £6.676m in 2025/26 to £2.675m in 2026/27 (a 60% reduction).

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Capital and Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Pooled fund investment losses (£0.561m) protected by statutory override until April 2029
findings.detail: The council holds £15m in pooled/diversified funds with accumulated unrealised losses of £0.561m. Currently, a statutory accounting override prevents these losses from impacting the revenue budget, but this override expires on 1 April 2029. After that date, any further losses would impact the revenue account directly unless covered by reserves. The council has appropriated £1.310m to a Treasury Capital Depreciation Reserve to mitigate this risk.
findings.matters: This creates a deferred revenue risk; once statutory protection ends, asset value fluctuations will directly impact the revenue budget unless reserves are sufficient to absorb them.
findings.figures: Current unrealised loss £0.561m; statutory override expires 1 April 2029; reserve appropriation £1.310m
findings.quote: The fluctuations in capital value of the pooled/diversified funds to date is a loss of £0.561m. This is currently reversed by the statutory override preventing any accounting loss impacting on the revenue accounts. This is due to end 1 April 2029.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Capital and Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Reserves declining over medium term; additional unknown costs from potential Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The council notes that usable reserves are declining over the medium term as they are used to finance both capital and revenue expenditure. Reserves will decrease further when unknown costs relating to Local Government Reorganisation impact the council. The council does not quantify these reorganisation costs or their timing.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's financial cushion and resilience against unexpected costs. Unquantified reorganisation costs represent a material budgeting uncertainty that could further strain an already-tightening reserve position.
findings.figures: Unquantified LGR costs; timing unknown
findings.quote: Reserves will decrease further when spending plans are finalised and unknown costs such as those relating to Local Government Reorganisation impact on the Council.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Capital and Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: New Homes Bonus discontinued; external grant funding shrinking
findings.detail: The council identifies that New Homes Bonus has been discontinued in the 2026/27 settlement, removing a source of grant funding for capital investment. Combined with the end of S106 education monies being paid to the council, external funding sources are materially reducing, requiring the council to fund capital programmes from reserves or internal resources.
findings.matters: Loss of grant income forces capital and revenue plans to become more dependent on reserves and internal resources, reducing financial flexibility and creating budget pressure.
findings.figures: New Homes Bonus (discontinued); S106 education monies (ceasing)
findings.quote: We now know New Homes Bonus has been discontinued in the 2026/27 finance settlement.

findings.headline: Capital programme underspent by 58%, with £4.3m budgets carried forward into 2025/26
findings.detail: The council budgeted £12.145m capital expenditure in 2024/25 but only spent £7.021m (42% of budget). The £5.125m variance, with £4.3m carried forward, raises questions about project readiness or delivery capacity, particularly given the large five-year capital programme of £27m.
findings.matters: Persistent capital slippage suggests either overly optimistic budgeting or delivery constraints; this affects the council's ability to execute its investment priorities
findings.figures: £12.145m budgeted; £7.021m spent; 42% execution rate; £5.125m variance; £4.3m carried to 2025/26
findings.quote: The year-end Capital Programme provision totalled £12.145m. Actual expenditure in relation to this provision totalled £7.021m (42% of the budget) giving rise to a variance of £5.125m. Budgets to the value of £4.3m have been carried forward into 2025/26.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves planned to reduce from £21m to £15m over the MTFS period
findings.detail: Reserves will be drawn down to deliver Corporate Priorities. While the council maintains adequate general reserves (£2.6m), the overall reserve buffer is expected to decline significantly, reducing financial flexibility for unexpected pressures or if risks (LGR, funding reform) materialise.
findings.matters: Declining reserves mean less room to absorb shocks; reserves are a council's primary tool to manage timing mismatches and unexpected demand
findings.figures: Reserves reducing from £21m to £15m; £6m reduction over 5-year MTFS period
findings.quote: Reserves are expected to be drawn upon to deliver the Council's Corporate Priorities with the balance reducing from £21m to £15m over the period of the MTFS

findings.headline: Five-year balanced budget assumes £3.5m windfall receipts in 2025/26 that depend on delayed Business Rates reform
findings.detail: The council's five-year surplus of only £0.172m is described as 'largely predicated on transferring windfall receipts of £3.5m in 2025/26' due to delays in Business Rates reform. If the windfall does not materialise, the remaining four years run at deficit and require reserve support.
findings.matters: A fragile plan dependent on a single windfall creates risk; if Business Rates reform proceeds or timelines change, the plan moves to structural deficit
findings.figures: £0.172m total 5-year surplus; £3.5m windfall receipts required in 2025/26; deficits in remaining years without the windfall
findings.quote: There is a total surplus position of £0.172m over the 5-year period which is largely predicated on transferring 'windfall receipts' £3.5m in 2025/26 (due to the delay of Business Rates reform and one additional year of NHB funding) into reserves to smooth out annual deficits in the remaining 4 years of the plan

findings.headline: Government funding reform threatens to cut the council's income, particularly if treated as relatively affluent
findings.detail: Early indications suggest potential funding reduction; the government views this council as relatively affluent compared to others. While the settlement is expected to cover more than one year, offering some certainty, the outcome of the reform consultation won't be known until the autumn Local Government Finance Settlement.
findings.matters: A reduction in grant funding is foundational risk; if materialised, it would force either additional savings or reserve drawdown beyond current MTFS planning
findings.figures: Amount of potential reduction not quantified in this document; settlement expected autumn 2025/26
findings.quote: However, early indications suggest a potential reduction in funding, as the Government views the Council as relatively affluent.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will require significant transition costs with funding limited
findings.detail: The council has allocated £0.661m from 2023/24 efficiencies plus proposes £0.456m from Q1 2025/26 efficiencies specifically for LGR transition. The document describes LGR as presenting 'the most significant challenges faced by the Council since the pandemic in 2020', though timing and final structure remain uncertain.
findings.matters: Reorganisation changes the entity itself and has material direct costs; unclear funding for transition creates budget pressure independent of normal operations
findings.figures: £0.661m allocated; £0.456m proposed; total £1.117m for LGR costs
findings.quote: Transition costs are expected to be significant, with limited new funding. To mitigate this risk, the Council has allocated £0.661m from 2023/24 efficiencies and proposes a further £0.456m from efficiencies identified at Quarter 1

findings.headline: New risk identified for loss of housing benefit subsidy on supported accommodation
findings.detail: A new operational risk (OR_FCS17) has been added to the register for supported accommodation provided by non-registered providers such as charities and Community Interest Companies, which could result in loss of housing benefit subsidy.
findings.matters: New supported accommodation ventures that rely on housing benefit subsidy carry financial risk if the subsidy conditions are not met or the provider fails; this is an emerging exposure
findings.figures: OR_FCS17
findings.quote: OR_FCS17 Loss of Housing Benefit subsidy - New Supported Accommodation provided by non-Registered Provider (Charity / CIC's) – loss of HB subsidy

findings.headline: Business rates income from Ratcliffe on Soar Power Station has been removed from the budget
findings.detail: What appears to have been a major business rates payer has been removed from the rating list. The council has set aside a provision to cover potential appeals and mitigates any associated risk, but the likelihood of other major ratepayers disappearing is considered low.
findings.matters: Loss of a major business rates payer materially affects the council's income base and financial stability; a lender needs to understand which large employers anchor the rates income
findings.figures: Business rates income from Ratcliffe on Soar Power Station removed
findings.quote: The business rates income received from Ratcliffe on Soar Power Station has now been removed from the budget. While it is considered unlikely that other major ratepayers will be removed from the rating list, a provision has been set aside to cover potential appeals and mitigate any associated risk.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for External Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: Bank reconciliation control issue from 2022/23 remains unresolved and is still being reviewed by the auditor
findings.detail: A £9,000 error identified in the 2022/23 bank reconciliation was carried forward into 2023/24 but was never corrected. The auditor is still awaiting responses to queries about the current year bank reconciliation and cannot yet conclude whether this control weakness has been resolved.
findings.matters: An unresolved reconciliation error from two years prior suggests persistent weakness in cash and bank control procedures, which is fundamental to financial control
findings.figures: £9,000 error outstanding since 2022/23
findings.quote: we found that the £9k error was brought forward into the 2023/24 bank reconciliation and had not yet been corrected.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for External Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: Multiple fixed assets remain on the register despite being no longer in use or disposed of, indicating a process control weakness
findings.detail: The auditor identified assets in the council's fixed asset register that should have been removed because they are no longer in use or have been disposed of. While the effect on the 2024/25 accounts is not material, it exceeds the trivial reporting threshold, and the auditor warns the impact could be material in future periods if controls are not strengthened.
findings.matters: Weak asset disposal controls suggest broader issues in the fixed asset management process and could result in material misstatements if not addressed
findings.figures: Impact above the trivial reporting threshold (£0.026m) but not material to 2024/25 accounts
findings.quote: We identified a number of assets within the Council's fixed asset register which should have been removed as they were no longer in use or had been disposed of.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for External Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: Council is preparing for Local Government Reorganisation which could affect its future structure and financial sustainability
findings.detail: The audit report identifies ongoing preparations for Local Government Reorganisation as a significant matter discussed with management during the audit. This restructuring could materially affect the council's financial position, operational capacity, and borrowing arrangements going forward, though the report provides no detail on timing or scope.
findings.matters: Reorganisation introduces structural change and uncertainty that could affect the council's financial sustainability, service delivery capacity, and ability to service debt
findings.figures: Not quantified in the report
findings.quote: Ongoing preparations for Local Government Reorganisation and the effect on Rushcliffe Borough Council.

findings.headline: Borrowing risk previously flagged now removed; no borrowing anticipated
findings.detail: Risk CRR_FCS31 (Borrowing costs) has been removed from the register. The note states: 'The Council do not anticipate needing to borrow in line with existing Medium Term Financial Strategy and associated reserves.' This indicates current reserve strength and no short-term debt need.
findings.matters: Absence of anticipated borrowing suggests adequate cash reserves and self-sufficiency; positive indicator for lender but dependent on sustained income from remaining sources.
findings.figures: Risk removed; no borrowing anticipated
findings.quote: The Council do not anticipate needing to borrow in line with existing Medium Term Financial Strategy and associated reserves.

findings.headline: Gamston supplementary planning document delayed, blocking coordinated development
findings.detail: The Gamston SPD approval is delayed due to resource and complexity constraints. Rated 9 (impact 3, likelihood 3). Mitigation describes engaging external consultants and working on planning performance agreements, suggesting active engagement but no firm timescale.
findings.matters: Planning delays reduce developer certainty and council income from s.106 contributions and CIL; affect long-term capital funding and housing delivery, key lender metrics.
findings.figures: Rating 9 (impact 3, likelihood 3); development delays; infrastructure gaps noted
findings.quote: Uncoordinated development takes place as a result of the Gamston supplementary planning document not being approved in a timely manner potentially leading to a disjointed community lacking in the necessary infrastructure

findings.headline: Rushcliffe Oaks Crematorium returns below business case forecast
findings.detail: The crematorium facility is experiencing lower-than-forecast cremation volumes, impacting its internal rate of return and extending return on investment timeline. Rated 6 (impact 3, likelihood 2), indicating a material capital asset not performing to plan.
findings.matters: Capital investment underperformance signals either demand forecasting weakness or market saturation; affects cash generation, reserve rebuilding, and capital receipts available for other schemes.
findings.figures: Rating 6; lower than forecast cremation volumes; extended payback period
findings.quote: Rushcliffe Oaks Crematorium not meeting the business model targets as a result of lower than forecast numbers of cremations being carried out, impacting on the internal rate of return and therefore longer return on investment

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates 16-rated risk to MTFS stability
findings.detail: Two risks rated 16 (the highest in the matrix: impact 4, likelihood 4) relate to Local Government Reorganisation. Risk CRR_FCS35 identifies destabilisation of the Medium Term Financial Strategy as a result of structural changes and transition to a new authority. Mitigation is only to participate in working groups and local discussions.
findings.matters: Highest-rated risks in the register signal fundamental uncertainty about the council's future financial structure and ability to plan; directly undermines lender confidence in 3-5 year financial forecasts.
findings.figures: Rating 16 (4 impact × 4 likelihood); two risks at this level
findings.quote: Risk to the Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) as a result of changes in the structure of local government and on transition to a new authority leading to destabilisation of the budget

findings.headline: New Homes Bonus funding ceased with no replacement
findings.detail: Government policy has ended New Homes Bonus allocation to the council with no replacement income. The risk register previously rated this at 9 (impact 3, likelihood 3); it is now reduced to 6 following the actual cessation. The register states the impact is mitigated now that the budget has been adjusted to zero.
findings.matters: Loss of predictable central government grant compounds income volatility; indicates reliance on volatile funding sources and impacts borrowing capacity and reserve sustainability.
findings.figures: NHB budget reduced to zero; risk rating 9 to 6
findings.quote: The budget for New Homes Bonus has been reduced to zero. The impact of NHB ceasing with no replacement is therefore mitigated.

findings.headline: Ratcliffe on Soar Power Station business rates removed from budget
findings.detail: The council has lost business rates income from a major ratepayer. The risk was previously rated at 9 (impact 3, likelihood 3) and now reduced to 6 following removal of this income from the budget. The register notes the likelihood of other major ratepayers being removed is considered unlikely.
findings.matters: Loss of a significant business rates payer directly reduces council revenue and complicates medium-term financial planning; affects debt sustainability ratios lenders use.
findings.figures: Rating reduced from 9 to 6; loss of one major power station ratepayer
findings.quote: The business rates income received from Ratcliffe on Soar Power Station has now been removed from the budget. The likelihood of other major ratepayers being removed from the rating list is considered unlikely.
